title: What are you doing this weekend?
content_html:
1. My workplace just announced the immediate end of working from home a couple of days a week, back to full time in the office; so I'll be looking at job postings.

    It's somewhat nice to have something concrete to stress over rather than the general malaise that seems to have settled over the entire software engineering field in recent months.

    1. Oh don't worry - the general malaise will still be there for you once you're no longer stressed about something concrete.

  2. licking my wounds after my first layoff, at the only company i’ve ever worked at full time

    1. Shitty feeling. I've been there though. It's not your fault.

  3. Today's the Seattle co-working session for Handmade devs. Swing by if you live nearby!

  4. Using Claude Code for some reverse engineering work. I just hit a major milestone in removing a kill switch. It really feels like we're in a golden age of game preservation.

    Aside from that, I'll probably paint something.

    Aspirationally I always feel like I should be learning more real-world stuff like more advanced physics or how to build a cold fusion reactor. The best futures are gated on energy and materials.

    1. Cool! What game?

  5. Relaxing from 9 hours of intense training this week.

    Will likely reach new heights of alertness once the exercise hangover/fogginess passes which I will use to get into content creation.

    Not entirely sure where to start, been a decade or so since I used After Effects/Premiere Elements/Movie Maker (yes, really) & in that time I've switched to Linux, and I'm expecting all video editors to be as frustrating as GIMP is for images and as Ardour2 is for audio, but I'm hoping to be pleasantly surprised.

    1. You really should be using Krita for images on Linux. It's miles ahead of GIMP.

      For video, my experience is thus:

      • Kdenlive is ok for basic editing.

      • Blender is the most stereotypical 2003 Linux experience you can have. This tool can do everything, and I do mean everything, you can even use it for programming, but absolutely nothing of it is intuitive or easy. Everything is contextual and stateful, and in each context and state everything is done with random keypresses that are not documented. Blender has some of the most batshit insane UX I have seen in my professional life.

      1. I'll be using Blender to model out some woodworking/furniture projects this weekend.

        I think that it differs the prevailing norm in that you have to actively learn it up front — there's no way to ease into it. But having done just enough of that, the scant 1% of it that I know has been an awesome tool.

        FWIW you can discover the keypresses through the menus. It's a real throwback in that way.

    2. It's a shame the guys over at https://blickeditor.com/ are prioritizing their Windows support before Linux, otherwise I would've recommended them for a new take on video editing software :( Both them and FilePilot are sadly married to the Windows ecosystem still for the foreseeable future.

  6. Got hit with a sudden layoff Wednesday, so will be looking at job positions. It’s so weird to be fired after receiving constant great feedback and getting more responsibility.

    If anyone has some openings I’d be glad to know.

  7. New Anthrodam! (On a slightly twisted ankle and/or pulled hamstring, alas!)

  8. Sailing with the eldest on Sunday, for our second outing in the newly acquired Wayfarer. Racing again, see if we can get any higher up the field than at the back. Fingers crossed for a little more wind.

    Need to upgrade mother's tech to Apple Silicon era, going from an iMac 27" to a Mac mini with Studio Display. Should be a blisteringly good upgrade for her.

    Fix some bits and pieces on cars no doubt as well. Got an ever growing pile of boxes in the hall that need fitting to the cars, servicing and quality of life things for the new (to us) Focus mostly.

  9. Will try to draft an article about my recent experimentation with Project Gemini and how I have re-published my blog under it.

  10. I finally implemented effects this week, and used them so my repl can just evaluate code as if it's all there at once, using a "more input required" effect to print the input prompt if more text is needed (instead of on every token, which was maddening).

    The whole thing feels fragile, though, and they're essentially bags of mutable global state, so I think they must be resumed in order to reinstate previous values. Not ideal! So for something more robust, I think I have a lot of light reading to do this weekend. I get the feeling "delimited continuations" are actually a lot less scary than they sound.

    1. I highly recommend the paper Direct implementation of shift and reset in the MinCaml compiler for the basic idea around implementing delimited control "directly". I found this paper to be the most straightforward of all the possible resources. Of course, in practice, you may wish to use a segmented stack (cactus stack) as, say, OCaml does (as of version 5).

      Of course, you can cut many corners if your implementation is not compiling to machine code. For example, you can effectively write an interpreter in CPS and use the "meta continuation" of the interpreter for delimited control.

      1. Oh, that looks very promising, thank you!

        It's an interpreter in Scheme so I should be able to cut several corners, but I'm trying to be careful not to preclude machine code compilation and the like.

  11. Playing Padel & playing GTAIV. Coding a little on my task management app.

  12. I got the itch to work on a project I've been thinking about for quite a while which looks like Perkeep but backed by a Datomic/Mentat-like database, and queriable with Datalog. Basically a logic database with extensions for blobs and tags so it can act like a cross of Perkeep, a tag-based filesystem, and Hydrus.

  13. Continue binge reading malazan (can't be arsed about life when there's a siege on)

  14. I've been working on CabFuse, a free tab manager for Windows 10 File Explorer.

    Recently added automatic merging of new Explorer windows into tabs and optional vertical tabs.

  15. Traveling down to Virginia to visit partner's family.

  16. After a week at the IETF 127 I am looking forward to being home and spending time with family.

    Will likely reach new heights of alertness once the exercise hangover/fogginess passes which I will use to get into content creation.

    Not entirely sure where to start, been a decade or so since I used After Effects/Premiere Elements/Movie Maker (yes, really) & in that time I've switched to Linux, and I'm expecting all video editors to be as frustrating as GIMP is for images and as Ardour2 is for audio, but I'm hoping to be pleasantly surprised.

      For video, my experience is thus:

      • Kdenlive is ok for basic editing.

      • Blender is the most stereotypical 2003 Linux experience you can have. This tool can do everything, and I do mean everything, you can even use it for programming, but absolutely nothing of it is intuitive or easy. Everything is contextual and stateful, and in each context and state everything is done with random keypresses that are not documented. Blender has some of the most batshit insane UX I have seen in my professional life.

      1. I'll be using Blender to model out some woodworking/furniture projects this weekend.

        I think that it differs the prevailing norm in that you have to actively learn it up front — there's no way to ease into it. But having done just enough of that, the scant 1% of it that I know has been an awesome tool.

        FWIW you can discover the keypresses through the menus. It's a real throwback in that way.

    2. It's a shame the guys over at https://blickeditor.com/ are prioritizing their Windows support before Linux, otherwise I would've recommended them for a new take on video editing software :( Both them and FilePilot are sadly married to the Windows ecosystem still for the foreseeable future.

• I finally implemented effects this week, and used them so my repl can just evaluate code as if it's all there at once, using a "more input required" effect to print the input prompt if more text is needed (instead of on every token, which was maddening).

    The whole thing feels fragile, though, and they're essentially bags of mutable global state, so I think they must be resumed in order to reinstate previous values. Not ideal! So for something more robust, I think I have a lot of light reading to do this weekend. I get the feeling "delimited continuations" are actually a lot less scary than they sound.

    1. I highly recommend the paper Direct implementation of shift and reset in the MinCaml compiler for the basic idea around implementing delimited control "directly". I found this paper to be the most straightforward of all the possible resources. Of course, in practice, you may wish to use a segmented stack (cactus stack) as, say, OCaml does (as of version 5).

      Of course, you can cut many corners if your implementation is not compiling to machine code. For example, you can effectively write an interpreter in CPS and use the "meta continuation" of the interpreter for delimited control.

      1. Oh, that looks very promising, thank you!

        It's an interpreter in Scheme so I should be able to cut several corners, but I'm trying to be careful not to preclude machine code compilation and the like.

1. My workplace just announced the immediate end of working from home a couple of days a week, back to full time in the office; so I'll be looking at job postings. It's somewhat nice to have something concrete to stress over rather than the general malaise that seems to have settled over the entire software engineering field in recent months. Oh don't worry - the general malaise will still be there for you once you're no longer stressed about something concrete.
  2. licking my wounds after my first layoff, at the only company i’ve ever worked at full time Shitty feeling. I've been there though. It's not your fault.
  3. Today's the Seattle co-working session for Handmade devs. Swing by if you live nearby!
  4. Using Claude Code for some reverse engineering work. I just hit a major milestone in removing a kill switch. It really feels like we're in a golden age of game preservation. Aside from that, I'll probably paint something. Aspirationally I always feel like I should be learning more real-world stuff like more advanced physics or how to build a cold fusion reactor. The best futures are gated on energy and materials. 凉爽的！ What game?
  5. Relaxing from 9 hours of intense training this week. Will likely reach new heights of alertness once the exercise hangover/fogginess passes which I will use to get into content creation. Not entirely sure where to start, been a decade or so since I used After Effects/Premiere Elements/Movie Maker (yes, really) & in that time I've switched to Linux, and I'm expecting all video editors to be as frustrating as GIMP is for images and as Ardour2 is for audio, but I'm hoping to be pleasantly surprised. You really should be using Krita for images on Linux. It's miles ahead of GIMP. For video, my experience is thus: Kdenlive is ok for basic editing. Blender is the most stereotypical 2003 Linux experience you can have. This tool can do everything, and I do mean everything, you can even use it for programming, but absolutely nothing of it is intuitive or easy. Everything is contextual and stateful, and in each context and state everything is done with random keypresses that are not documented. Blender has some of the most batshit insane UX I have seen in my professional life. I'll be using Blender to model out some woodworking/furniture projects this weekend. I think that it differs the prevailing norm in that you have to actively learn it up front — there's no way to ease into it. But having done just enough of that, the scant 1% of it that I know has been an awesome tool. FWIW you can discover the keypresses through the menus. It's a real throwback in that way. It's a shame the guys over at https://blickeditor.com/ are prioritizing their Windows support before Linux, otherwise I would've recommended them for a new take on video editing software :( Both them and FilePilot are sadly married to the Windows ecosystem still for the foreseeable future.
  6. Got hit with a sudden layoff Wednesday, so will be looking at job positions. It’s so weird to be fired after receiving constant great feedback and getting more responsibility. If anyone has some openings I’d be glad to know.
  7. New Anthrodam! (On a slightly twisted ankle and/or pulled hamstring, alas!)
  8. Sailing with the eldest on Sunday, for our second outing in the newly acquired Wayfarer. Racing again, see if we can get any higher up the field than at the back. Fingers crossed for a little more wind. Need to upgrade mother's tech to Apple Silicon era, going from an iMac 27" to a Mac mini with Studio Display. Should be a blisteringly good upgrade for her. Fix some bits and pieces on cars no doubt as well. Got an ever growing pile of boxes in the hall that need fitting to the cars, servicing and quality of life things for the new (to us) Focus mostly.
